Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament

Why a pure major third does not beat and the piano’s does, the syntonic and Pythagorean commas, and what twelve equal steps cost. Hear both on sine waves, the drone and a chord keyboard, then meet meantone, well temperaments and tunings that are not twelve-note.

A piano is slightly out of tune on purpose. Every chord on it, apart from the octave, is a little wrong, and the wrongness is spread so evenly that all twelve keys sound alike. The alternative is just intonation (JI), where intervals are tuned to the simple ratios that the harmonic series gives you, and they sound smooth and still. This lesson shows what each costs, with ears first and numbers second.

How to use the page. Every widget has a ▶ button. The bar at the bottom of the window sets the volume (start low). The Drone button in the top navigation bar is the same drone as the one on this page. Click a heading to fold a section away, or use On this page on the right to jump (shift-click folds the others). The lesson on the harmonic series goes further into where the ratios come from.

The harmonic series gives the ratios

A note on a real instrument is a stack of frequencies at whole-number multiples of the lowest, the fundamental: 1×, 2×, 3×, 4×, and so on. Those are the harmonics. Each interval between neighbouring harmonics is a simple ratio of whole numbers:

Between harmonics Ratio Interval
1 and 2 2:1 Octave
2 and 3 3:2 Perfect fifth
3 and 4 4:3 Perfect fourth
4 and 5 5:4 Major third
5 and 6 6:5 Minor third

Harmonics 4, 5 and 6 together are a major triad, 4:5:6. That is the reason a major chord sounds stable: it is already inside every note you hear. Below, the first sixteen harmonics are written out over any root, with how many cents each is from the nearest piano note. A cent is 1/100 of a piano half step, so an octave is 1200 cents. Press Harmonic, then tempered and listen to the harmonics that are most out of tune with the piano (7, 11, 13 and 14).

Frequencies multiply, but we hear pitch by ratio: going up a fifth always multiplies the frequency by 3/2, whether you start on a low note or a high one. To compare ratios, take 1200 × log₂(ratio) to get cents. A pure fifth, 3:2, is 1200 × log₂(1.5) = 701.96 cents. A pure major third, 5:4, is 386.31 cents.

Why pure intervals do not beat

When two notes are close in frequency, their waves line up and then fall out of step, over and over. The sound swells and fades at a rate equal to the difference in their frequencies. That is a beat: 440 Hz with 443 Hz beats three times a second.

Beating also happens between the harmonics of two different notes. In a pure major third (4:5), the 5th harmonic of the lower note and the 4th harmonic of the upper note are exactly the same frequency, so they simply reinforce each other. When the interval is slightly off, those two harmonics are a few hertz apart and beat. A pure fifth (2:3) has the same matching harmonics, the 3rd of the lower note and the 2nd of the upper.

The widget shows it. With Only the two harmonics that should match the sound is just two sine waves, and the picture is their sum: it swells and fades as they drift in and out of step. Switch the tuning between Just and Equal temperament and hear the beating start and stop. The wavy line is drawn slowed down; the real rate is in the text under the controls.

Now the same with all the harmonics of two notes, which is what a real chord does. Choose another interval with the Interval menu. Notice that the fifth beats slowly (it is only 2 cents off) and the thirds and sixths beat fast (14 to 16 cents off). That is why equal temperament is so much kinder to fifths than to thirds.

Two commas: why tuning cannot be perfect

Pure tuning runs into arithmetic. Two facts about ratios cannot both be true:

  • Stack twelve pure fifths (3:2) and you arrive at the note seven octaves up, almost. Twelve fifths are (3/2)¹² = 129.746; seven octaves are 2⁷ = 128. The gap is the Pythagorean comma, 531441:524288, or 23.46 cents, nearly a quarter of a half step.
  • Stack four pure fifths and reduce by two octaves and you get a major third, but a wide one: 81:64 (407.8 cents), compared with the pure 5:4 (386.3 cents). The difference, 81:80 or 21.51 cents, is the syntonic comma.

So the pure thirds of the harmonic series (5:4) and the pure fifths (3:2) are made of different building blocks, and they do not fit together. A tuning system is a decision about which of those to keep and which to spoil.

Just intonation, and why it cannot modulate

In a just scale, every note is a whole-number ratio of the tonic (Do). The common major scale version is:

Do Re Mi Fa Sol La Ti Do
1 9/8 5/4 4/3 3/2 5/3 15/8 2

The I, IV and V chords (Do–Mi–Sol, Fa–La–Do, Sol–Ti–Re) are pure 4:5:6 triads, and they sound beautifully still. The trouble starts with the other chords. The ii chord is Re–Fa–La: from Re (9/8) to La (5/3) the ratio is (5/3) ÷ (9/8) = 40/27, which is 680.4 cents. That is a fifth 21.5 cents flat, a syntonic comma off, and it sounds sour. To get a good ii chord you would need a different Re (10/9), but then the notes of V would be wrong. In the key of C, the note D has two jobs and a different pure frequency for each.

That is the main limit of just intonation on a fixed-pitch instrument (a keyboard, a fretted guitar, a marimba). Tune the keyboard for C major and the same keys give poor chords in D major or E♭ major. You would want more than 12 notes per octave, or a retune for each key. Voices, violins, trombones and other instruments that can adjust each note do this naturally: a choir singing Do–Mi–Sol will tune the triad pure, and a progression like C – Am – Dm – G – C will drift upward in pitch by a syntonic comma over each lap if every chord is tuned pure.

Here is the drone, held on Do with Mi and Sol above it (a major triad). Pure tunes Mi to 5/4 and Sol to 3/2 of Do; Equal uses the piano’s notes. Switch back and forth while it sounds. Listen for the third: in the pure setting the chord sits still, and in equal temperament it has a faint shimmer, the beating from the last section.

Try this: with the drone sounding, sing or play (on any instrument that can bend its pitch) the note Mi above the drone, first sliding toward the piano’s version, then toward the pure one. The pure one locks into the drone. It is the pitch that stops beating.

Equal temperament: twelve equal steps

Equal temperament (12-TET) solves the key problem by making every half step the same size. An octave is a 2:1 ratio and has twelve steps, so each step multiplies the frequency by 2^(1/12) = 1.059463. A semitone is exactly 100 cents, and every interval of the same size is the same in every key. Twelve fifths then come out to exactly seven octaves, and the Pythagorean comma is spread evenly: each fifth is narrowed by 23.46 ÷ 12 = 1.96 cents.

The price is that no interval except the octave is pure. The fifth is only 2 cents flat, which is close enough to ignore. But the thirds and sixths are 14 to 16 cents off, enough to hear:

Interval Just ratio Just (cents) Equal (cents) Equal minus just
Minor second 16:15 111.7 100 −11.7
Major second 9:8 203.9 200 −3.9
Minor third 6:5 315.6 300 −15.6
Major third 5:4 386.3 400 +13.7
Perfect fourth 4:3 498.0 500 +2.0
Tritone 45:32 590.2 600 +9.8
Perfect fifth 3:2 702.0 700 −2.0
Minor sixth 8:5 813.7 800 −13.7
Major sixth 5:3 884.4 900 +15.6
Minor seventh 9:5 1017.6 1000 −17.6
Major seventh 15:8 1088.3 1100 +11.7
Octave 2:1 1200 1200 0

In words: the tempered major third is about 14 cents sharp of the pure 5:4, the tempered fifth about 2 cents flat of 3:2, and the tempered minor third about 16 cents flat of 6:5. Thirds are the most exposed because the ear uses them to decide whether a chord is major or minor, and because the beating of two harmonics (the 5th and the 4th) falls in a region where the ear is most sensitive. The minor sixth and the major sixth are the thirds turned upside down, so they are wrong by the same amount.

Equal temperament is the standard for the piano, the guitar, MIDI and nearly every synthesizer. Its strength is that it lets you play in any key, modulate anywhere, and use chromatic and jazz harmony that no pure system supports. Many singers, string players and brass players move toward just intonation while they play, without thinking about it.

Pure chords from the key note are smooth; notice what happens in the pure setting with D minor (D, F, A): that is the ii chord from above, and the pure fifth D–A is not available.

Other systems, briefly

Equal temperament is one answer to the comma problem, and not the only one used.

  • Pythagorean tuning. All fifths are pure 3:2, and the thirds come out wide (81:64, 407.8 cents, 21.5 cents sharp of 5:4). It suits melody, with its sharp leading tones and bright, tense thirds, and it was the system of medieval Europe, whose music was built on fifths and fourths. One fifth, the wolf, is out by the Pythagorean comma (678.5 cents).
  • Quarter-comma meantone. Renaissance and early Baroque keyboards narrowed each fifth by a quarter of a syntonic comma (696.6 cents) so that the major thirds came out pure (386.3 cents). Chords in the home keys are lovely. The cost is an even worse wolf fifth (about 737.6 cents), and keys with many sharps or flats are unusable.
  • Well temperaments (Werckmeister, Vallotti, Kirnberger and others). Eighteenth-century tunings that spread the comma unevenly so that every key works but each has its own colour: keys near C have nearly pure thirds, and distant keys are tenser. In Werckmeister III four fifths (C–G, G–D, D–A, B–F♯) are narrowed by a quarter of the Pythagorean comma and the rest are pure. In Vallotti six fifths (F–C–G–D–A–E–B) are narrowed by a sixth of the comma and the rest are pure. Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier (1722) has a prelude and fugue in all 24 keys, so it needs a tuning where every key is playable. Its exact temperament is still debated; “well tempered” did not mean equal. Many listeners find these keys have individual character, which equal temperament flattens.
  • Equal temperament gradually took over in the nineteenth century, as chromatic harmony and modulation made key colour impossible to keep.

Beyond twelve notes

Not all music divides the octave into twelve.

  • Arabic maqam. Many maqamat use the “neutral” second and third, about halfway between a minor and a major one (roughly 150 and 350 cents), notated with a half-flat sign. This is often described as quarter tones (24 notes to the octave), but the actual pitches vary by maqam, region and performer, and are set by ear.
  • Equal divisions other than 12. 19-TET has an almost pure minor third (315.8 cents against the 6:5 of 315.6) but a weak fifth (694.7). 31-TET has near-pure major thirds (387.1 cents) and a good fifth (696.8), and was proposed in the 16th century to improve on meantone. 53-TET has a fifth within 0.07 cent of 3:2 and a major third within 1.4 cents, which is why it is a favourite for theorists approximating just intonation. All need special keyboards or a computer.
  • Gamelan. Indonesian ensembles use two scales, five-note slendro (roughly equal steps of about 240 cents) and seven-note pelog (unequal steps, normally five of the seven in a piece). Every ensemble is tuned to itself, and no two are the same, so the instruments belong together. Paired instruments are often tuned slightly apart on purpose to give a shimmering beat, the ombak (“wave”), the same beating you heard above, used as a colour rather than avoided.

Seeing it: a strobe tuner, pure intervals, and why pianos are stretched

A needle tuner gives one number. A strobe tuner gives one row of moving stripes for every partial of the note you play. Row k listens at k times the pitch you are aiming at (the microphone signal is multiplied by a sine and cosine at that frequency and averaged; the phase of the result moves the stripes). If that partial is exactly where it should be, its stripes stand still. If it is sharp they drift to the right, and if flat to the left, at a speed equal to the error in Hz. Rows fade where the partial is weak, and the first tenth of a second of each note is ignored, because the attack is not a steady pitch.

Choose the target below: the equal-tempered note, a just interval over a tonic you pick, a step of 31-ET, or any number of cents above the note (350 is a neutral third). The conventional readout (nearest note and cents) is underneath. The microphone is asked for only when you press Start, and Stop lets it go. No microphone? The made-up string is a stack of oscillators you can detune.

Hear just intervals. With the tonic on A, the note E is aimed at 3:2 over A. Play (or sing) an E against an A drone (the Drone button in the top bar): when the beats stop, your E is the pure fifth, and every row stands still. It is about 2 cents wider than the piano’s E. Change the tonic to C: the target E is now the pure major third, 5:4, which is about 14 cents narrower than the piano’s. That is the number behind the beating in the widgets above, and the reason a choir with no keyboard drifts toward pure intervals.

Why a piano is stretched. The harmonic series of an ideal string is exactly 1, 2, 3, 4… times the fundamental. A real string has stiffness, so it resists bending near its ends, and the effect grows quickly with the partial number: partial k sounds at about k f √(1 + B k²), where B is the string’s inharmonicity (a mid-range piano string has B of the order of 0.0001 to 0.001, and the short thick bass strings and the shortest treble strings have more). Every upper partial is therefore sharp of the exact multiple. When two notes an octave apart are tuned, the beats a tuner listens to are between the upper note’s fundamental and the lower note’s second partial, which is already slightly sharp: so the upper note is tuned a little sharp of 2:1, and so on up the keyboard. The bass ends up flat and the treble sharp of the equal-tempered scale. This is called stretch tuning. Try it: set the source to the made-up string, press Start, and raise the stiffness. Row 1 stays still and the higher rows drift to the right, row 6 more than row 2. Notice that the readout above the bands, which reduces the whole sound to one pitch, is pulled sharp by the upper partials, while row 1 shows that the fundamental has not moved.

Things to try

  1. In the major-third widget, set the lower note to 110 Hz, then 440 Hz. At which pitch is the tempered third’s beating faster? (The beat rate is in Hz, so it doubles per octave.)
  2. In the second widget, step through the intervals in Equal temperament mode and rank them from most to least beating. The fifth and fourth should be at one end and the thirds and sixths at the other.
  3. Start the drone on Do with Mi and Sol, set to Pure, and hum along. Switch to Equal and hum again. Can you feel your pitch pulled toward the pure Mi?
  4. Play a D minor chord in the chord keyboard in just intonation and in equal temperament. Which sounds worse, and why? (The fifth D–A is 21.5 cents flat in the pure scale.)
  5. In the stiff-string tuner, set the stiffness to 0 and then to 0.0020. At which row does the drift first pass 10 cents? (Row k is sharp by 600 × log₂(1 + B k²) cents, from the formula above.)
  6. Calculate for yourself: the cents between two frequencies is 1200 × log₂(f₂ ÷ f₁). Check that A at 440 Hz and E at 660 Hz (a pure fifth) is 701.96 cents, and that the piano’s E is 659.26 Hz.
